extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on drafting and examining patent claims for definiteness, proper claim formats, and related 35 U.S.C. §112 issues (functional language, Markush groups, negative limitations, multiplicity, product-by-process, etc.). Intended to direct examiner treatment and applicant responses during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language in a claim can be permissible but may render a claim indefinite if it fails to provide a clear-cut indication of scope or merely states a problem to be solved or a result obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider context (specification disclosure and knowledge of a person of ordinary skill). Functional limitations that do not recite the particular structure, materials, or steps accomplishing the function may encompass all means or methods of resolving the problem and thus may not be supported by the written description or commensurate with the enabling disclosure (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph). Examples: claims reciting only intended results like 'aesthetically pleasing' were indefinite (Datamize); 'fragile gel' held indefinite where defined functionally (Halliburton); but 'transparent to infrared rays' was definite where specification showed consistent transmission (Swinehart). Examiners should consider whether the limitation gives clear scope, sets defined boundaries versus stating only a problem/result, and whether one skilled in the art would know what structures/steps are encompassed. During prosecution ambiguity may be resolved by: (1) using a quantitative metric (numeric limitation); (2) showing the specification provides a formula plus examples that meet/do not meet the limitation; (3) showing the specification gives general guidelines and examples sufficient for a skilled artisan; or (4) amending to recite particular structure that accomplishes the function. See 35 U.S.C. 112(b) vs 112(a) distinctions, relevant case law (Ariad, Hyatt, Halliburton, Marosi, Oakley) and MPEP §§2161-2164.08(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush groups / alternative limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a list of alternatives (a Markush group) is an acceptable claim form and should not automatically be rejected as confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112(b); treatment depends on whether the group is closed or open and whether the metes and bounds are ascertainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markush grouping = closed list (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C'). If the group is open-ended (uses 'comprising' or 'consisting essentially of') and is intended to be a selection from a list, it can be indefinite because other alternatives are unclear (In re Kiely). If combinations/mixtures of members are intended, include qualifying language (e.g., 'at least one member', 'or mixtures thereof'). A large number of alternatives does not by itself make a Markush claim indefinite (breadth is not indefiniteness), but if the group is so expansive that a skilled artisan cannot determine the metes and bounds (e.g., massive number of distinct chemical compounds), reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Double inclusion within a Markush group (redundant or overlapping members) is not per se improper — evaluate facts (Eli Lilly v. Teva example). See MPEP §2117, §803.02 and cited cases (Abbott Labs, Gardner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the term 'optionally' in alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of 'optionally' to indicate an alternative member in a list can be acceptable provided there is no ambiguity as to which alternatives are covered by the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'containing A, B, and optionally C' leaves no ambiguity, it is acceptable (Ex parte Cordova, Ex parte Wu). If the list of alternatives can vary and ambiguity arises about coverage, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is proper and should explain the confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative limitations (claiming what the invention is not) are not inherently ambiguous and are permissible so long as the boundaries of the claimed protection are set forth definitely and the negative limitation has basis in the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older case law criticized negative limitations, but current view permits them if definite (e.g., 'free from the proteins…' held definite in Wakefield). Any negative limitation/exclusionary proviso must have basis in the original disclosure; positive recitation of alternatives in the specification may be explicitly excluded in the claims. Silence generally will not suffice to support a negative limitation, but in some circumstances a skilled artisan may understand a negative limitation to be necessarily present (see Ex parte Parks, Novartis quoting Ariad). If lacking basis in the original disclosure, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as failing written description. See In re Schechter, In re Johnson, Inphi v. Netlist and MPEP §§2163-2163.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Old combination (do not reject on this ground)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be rejected on the non-statutory ground of 'old combination'; claims should instead be judged by statutory provisions such as 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical doctrine (Lincoln Engineering) is no longer a proper basis for rejection following the 1952 Patent Act. A rejection for old combination required a single reference disclosing a combination functioning substantially the same, but current practice is to evaluate claims under the statutory language (pointing out and distinctly claiming). See In re Bernhart, Ex parte Barber, Radio Steel and Mfg. Co., and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation (do not reject on this ground)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be rejected on the non-statutory ground of 'aggregation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregation rejections are non-statutory (In re Gustafson, In re Collier). If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements as defined in the specification, examine under appropriate statutory grounds and MPEP §2172.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolix claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be rejected as prolix only when overly long recitations or unimportant details render the scope of the claimed invention indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject for prolixity when long recitations prevent determination of the metes and bounds of the claimed subject matter. Apply carefully to avoid improper limitation of applicants' drafting latitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity / Undue multiplicity of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one claim may be presented provided claims differ substantially and are not unduly multiplied; unreasonable repetition or an excessive number of claims that confuse rather than clarify may warrant rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. 1.75 requires claims to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter. Undue multiplicity rejections should be rare and applied judiciously. If appropriate, examiner should call applicant, explain the issue, and request selection of a specified number of claims for examination; follow-up procedure for Office action and applicant selection is provided to preserve review rights before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. It's possible to reject one claim over an allowed claim where they are substantial duplicates (Ex parte Whitelaw, Ex parte Kochan). See In re Chandler and In re Flint for guidance on 'rule of reason.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Double inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no per se rule forbidding double inclusion (the same element appearing more than once) in a claim; whether it renders a claim indefinite depends on the facts and reasonable claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each case to determine whether multiple inclusion creates indefiniteness. Automatic application of a 'rule against' or 'allowing' double inclusion is improper. In some situations (e.g., device claims where an element is effectively recited twice) the claim may be indefinite (see In re Kelly, Ex parte Kristensen). Earlier Board decisions should be applied with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims (product claims defined in terms of the process by which they are made) are proper, provided it is clear the claim is directed to the product and not the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product, apparatus, manufacture, or composition claim may reference a process in which it is intended to be used without objection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), so long as clarity is maintained that the claim is to the product. Applicants may present claims of varying scope, including product-by-process terms when necessary. See Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma, In re Luck, In re Pilkington, In re Steppan, and Ex parte Pantzer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims combining product and process (product and process in same claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim that combines an apparatus/product and method steps (product and process) is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that mix statutory classes (e.g., a system claim that includes actions by users) create confusion about when direct infringement occurs and are therefore indefinite (Katz Interactive Call Processing Litigation, IPXL Holdings v. Amazon). Example: a system claim requiring a user action can be unclear whether infringement occurs upon making the system or upon user action. Ex parte Lyell and related decisions address such indefiniteness.
